column4: I follow a system prompt for compiling English glosses of spoken European Portuguese word-frequency entries. Verbatim summary: I must respond with valid JSON only (no markdown, no text before or after, single line). Fields: 'gloss' — one to three English senses, most frequent first, separated by '; ', at most six words per sense including any parenthesised disambiguator, verbs glossed with 'to', everything else bare and lower case, gloss only the given part of speech, multi-word entries glossed as a unit. 'example_pt' — one of the numbered corpus sentences copied exactly character for character including punctuation, capitalisation, missing accents and leading dashes; no invented, translated, corrected or shortened sentences; choose the shortest sentence clearly showing the first sense, preferring one a learner could follow; leave empty if no sentence will do (none given, none containing the entry in that part of speech, or the clearest are unintelligible, fragments, or need missing context). 'example_en' — a natural English translation of the chosen sentence, empty when example_pt is empty. 'flags' — a list, empty when none applies, from: vulgar (swearword, sexual or scatological), bp-leaning (mainly Brazilian), archaic (dated), name-like (probably mostly a proper name), uncertain (not confident or sentences do not settle the meaning). On reading the corpus: slang and vulgarities get plain, accurate glosses; do not euphemise, do not drop an offensive sense, do not add warnings since flags carries vulgar. Sentences are isolated subtitle lines picked independently, so consecutive numbers are unrelated and none continues another; they are noisy with missing or wrong accents, OCR slips, run-together words, speaker dashes and occasional nonsense — read past the noise and do not let one bad line override the obvious gloss. Spelling follows the 1990 orthographic agreement as used in Portugal; where an entry is an older spelling of a current word, gloss the word. The list is ranked by frequency in the Portugal-tagged half of OpenSubtitles, so the language is conversational and often informal. Each request gives one entry and up to twenty sentences; 'pos' is the tagger's majority reading, and where a word appears twice, 'share' gives the proportion of occurrences for that reading.
